Hardware security · Project overview

Power side-channel attack on RISC-V

Studying power leakage and physical key recovery on software AES-128 running on a RISC-V processor implemented on FPGA.

Omer Nachmani · B.Sc. final project · Ongoing research

Overview

This B.Sc. final project investigates power side-channel attacks against software AES-128 executed on a PicoRV32 RISC-V processor running on a ChipWhisperer CW305 Artix-7 FPGA. Because encryption runs as unoptimized C firmware on the CPU rather than in a dedicated hardware core, the measured power trace captures instruction execution, memory accesses, and surrounding SoC activity.

The platform integrates PicoRV32 (RV32IM with hardware multiplication enabled) with a 32 KiB unified byte-writable BRAM holding program code, data, and host plaintext/ciphertext mailboxes, a memory-mapped hardware trigger and completion unit at 0xFF000000, and a custom RSCV USB register bank with build-identity checks before every capture session.

Experimental platform

Components and measurement configuration of the research platform
ComponentImplementation
Processor and memoryPicoRV32 (RV32IM, MUL enabled) with 32 KiB unified byte-writable BRAM and mailbox ABI
WorkloadSoftware FIPS-197 AES-128 (-O0, ~181,092 cycles full encryption; 1,865-cycle first-round SubBytes trigger window)
FPGA targetChipWhisperer CW305 (Artix-7 XC7A100T), PLL1 at 10 MHz, 1.0 V VCCINT (~2,003 LUTs, 1,656 FFs, 16 RAMB36)
Capture equipmentChipWhisperer Husky (12-bit ADC at 40 MS/s, 34 dB gain, 16,000 samples/trace, memory-mapped trigger)
Verification and toolingCustom RTL wrappers and register bank, Icarus Verilog, Verilator, GTKWave, Vivado, RISC-V GCC, Python CPA pipeline

Before physical acquisition, the SoC and register path were verified in simulation against four OpenSSL AES known-answer vectors and 78 register-protocol checks, followed by timing-clean routed bitstreams and four hardware bring-up checkpoints on the CW305 confirming cycle-exact execution and trigger timing.

Baseline attack results

Two independent physical acquisition sessions of 1,024 traces each were captured on the CW305 using disjoint balanced plaintext schedules, with a full USB reset and bitstream reprogramming between sessions. Attack traces targeted the 1,865-cycle first-round SubBytes window (7,460 ADC samples at 40 MS/s) with no trace alignment or preprocessing.

First-round Correlation Power Analysis (CPA) using the Hamming-weight S-Box leakage model HW(SBox(plaintext[i] XOR key[i])) recovered all 16/16 AES-128 key bytes in both sessions, reaching full-key recovery at 96 traces (winning |r| between 0.56 and 0.66 versus runner-up values near 0.18, with 16/16 agreement across disjoint 512-trace halves).

Peak correlation points occurred evenly spaced by 436 ADC samples (109 target cycles) at identical positions across both sessions, directly matching the 16 byte-wise S-Box table lookups in software. Independent validation confirmed 1,024/1,024 ciphertext reproductions per session and 16/16 additional held-out ciphertexts reproduced using only the recovered key.

Hardware countermeasures

To be continued…

The current stage evaluates hardware protection architectures integrated into the RISC-V processor to defend software AES-128 against power side-channel attacks. Candidate directions under assessment include dummy execution and controlled power-noise hiding, randomized pipeline or memory timing delays, share-aware shadow register storage and operand masking, temporal shuffling, and custom RISC-V or vector extensions.

Selected prototypes will be evaluated against matched controls to compare leakage reduction and recovery effort against execution time and FPGA resource cost.
